title: What does the Lord require? (Micah 6:8)
hookLine: do justly, love mercy, walk humbly with your God
last: MERCY IS WIDER THAN YOU LIKE.

lines: A COURTROOM, THE MOUNTAINS AS JURY.
cards: Micah chapter six is set in a courtroom. God has a case against the people and calls the mountains and hills as the jury. God lays out years of care: I brought you out of Egypt, I sent you Moses, Aaron and Miriam.
Then a voice from the crowd answers, nervous, trying to settle. What do I bring? The offer starts climbing, like someone haggling against themselves.
Calves? Thousands of rams? Ten thousand rivers of oil?
My own firstborn child? An auction of guilt, every bid more extravagant than the last. Then the prophet cuts it off.

teach.h: HE HATH SHEWED THEE: YOU KNOW IT.
teach.b: The answer, in the King James Bible: "He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?" He hath shewed thee.
The answer isn't a secret; it has already been shown, and it was never more rams. Three things.
Do justly: action, the same justice Amos wanted rolling like a river, fair dealing, especially for people with no power.
Love mercy. The Hebrew word here is chesed: loyal, steady kindness, the love that keeps its promises. And Micah doesn't say do mercy.
He says love it. Enjoy it. Want it.
Then walk humbly with your God. Walk, not sit, not arrive: a whole life lived side by side, at God's pace.
The Hebrew word for humbly turns up almost nowhere else, and some readers hear in it something quiet and careful, not putting on a show.
One way to hold the three: each is a different part of a person, the hands, the heart, the feet.

teach.h: WHAT DOTH THE LORD REQUIRE OF THEE?
teach.b: Jews have treasured this verse too. The Talmud records a teaching that the prophets kept summing up the Torah's many commandments into fewer and fewer, and Micah brought them down to three.
Some Christians hear in it the same shape as Jesus's summary of the law: love God, love your neighbor. Short enough for a fridge magnet, big enough for a lifetime.

how: Christians read Micah 6:8 in worship and sing it in hymns and songs, and Christian service and justice groups use it as a summary of faith in action.

o: the fear of being judged in God's courtroom
loyal, steady kindness that keeps its promises
a strict rule about what to offer at the temple

games.q: what's inside Micah 6:8 — tap the pairs.
p: the feet: a life beside God

s: Micah says God wants bigger offerings
the bids climb to thousands of rams and rivers of oil, and Micah cuts them off: do justly, love mercy, walk humbly.
the word for mercy in Micah 6:8 is chesed
chesed means loyal, steady kindness: the love that keeps its promises.
he says love mercy: want it, enjoy it, not just perform it.

games.q: you're in God's courtroom with the mountains as jury. you want to settle the case. what do you bring?
o: thousands of rams and rivers of oil.
nothing new: do justly, love mercy, walk humbly.
games.why: Micah stops the bidding: "he hath shewed thee, O man, what is good." the answer was already known, and costs a life, not a herd.

practice: Say the three slowly in your head, justly, mercy, humbly, hands, heart, feet, and notice which one tugs at you: a fair thing you owe someone, a grudge you could set down, a need to perform or be right.
Choose just one, and picture the moment today when you'll practice it: the room, the person, the hour. If you pray, offer that one choice to God; if not, just hold the picture steady.

wordCard.voice: Chesed. Hebrew for loyal, steadfast kindness: the mercy Micah says to love, beside doing justly and walking humbly with your God.

orig.note: Hebrew: loyal, steadfast kindness. the mercy Micah says to love.

carryVoice: Your line: justly, mercy, humbly. The hands, the heart and the feet, all three. See you tomorrow.
